newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Meciar policies cost Slovakia NATO place -- rival.
newsitem.headline: Meciar policies cost Slovakia NATO place -- rival.

text.p: A Slovak opposition deputy said on Monday that Slovakia's failure to become a strong candidate for the first round of NATO expansion showed the shortcomings of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's foreign policy.
Over the weekend the independent daily Sme quoted Meciar as telling a rally of his supporters that the country had dropped out of the first round of NATO enlargement.
Slovakia's official policy has been to become one of the first new members of NATO, but its chances appeared to wane after U.S. and European Union criticism of the pace of democratic reform.
"So far only the Poles can feel sure (of their acceptance by NATO), Czechs probably, and Hungarians maybe. We (Slovakia) are more or less out of the running," he said.
The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary are widely tipped to be invited to join the security alliance after a NATO summit in Madrid in July.
Meciar's admission follows a summit meeting between U.S. President Bill Clinton and his Russian counterpart Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki last week where NATO expansion was a key issue.
But it found little sympathy among Slovak opposition parties, who said it was a result of his disastrous and controversial domestic and foreign policy.

"Meciar's government is failing to fulfil its most important commitment in the field of foreign policy," Vladimir Palko, deputy chairman of the opposition Christian-Democratic Movement (KDH), told Reuters.
"Every normal and decent politician would deduce personal consequences from this, but I don't expect Meciar to do it," he added.
Despite Meciar's pessimism, his ruling Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS) on Sunday recommended its supporters to vote in favour of joining NATO in a referendum set for May 23 and 24.

The opposition says the referendum, which asks if voters support membership and whether they favour nuclear weapons or foreign troops in Slovakia, is phrased to elicit a vote against membership to cover up the government's failure to be included in the first wave.
